title: Ericsson: 5G must shift focus from consumers to citizens, says UK chief
snippet: The future of 5G in the UK depends on recognising mobile networks as critical national infrastructure and moving beyond the narrow confines of consumer connectivity, according to Nadine Allen, Ericsson's Head of UK. The post Ericsson: 5G must shift focus from consumers to citizens, says UK chief appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Interview

The future of 5G in the UK depends on recognising mobile networks as critical national infrastructure and moving beyond the narrow confines of consumer connectivity, according to Nadine Allen, Ericsson’s Head of UK.

Speaking at Ericsson’s Elevate 5G event, Allen acknowledged the industry’s 5G revenue gap so far, arguing that 5G SA offers a major opportunity to revitalise 5G through the creation of new commercial models and the integration ofAI.

She called for a shift in perspective, moving away from what consumers want towards what citizens and critical services need.

“We need to shift away from a consumer focus to a citizen focus,” said Nadine. “That means anticipating not what users want from a network, but what they need from a network.”

The UK’s Emergency Services Network (ESN) is a perfect model for this type of collaboration between government and industry, wth Nadine suggesting similar approaches could benefit rail, energy, and defence.

“There are a number of industries that are either in the course of or due to go through quite significant transformation where I think the ESN model or similar can come into play,” said Nadine. “If we look at rail, for example, today on a 2G-based system, they’re moving to the Future Railway Mobile Communication System (FRMCS), which is based on 5G standards. We expect some commercial activity coming up in the foreseeable future for railways.”

The interview also touched on how AI is evolving in the UK and why robust wireless networks will be crucial to its ongoing growth and success.

“We are seeing AI move from data centres to distributed systems. And in order for those things to happen or to be brought to life in a meaningful way, we really have to ensure that we have very solid connectivity and underlying performance in networks,” said Nadine.

Watch the full interview to hear Nadine’s assessment of the UK’s 5G opportunity and what needs to happen next.

title: Ericsson demos counter-drone and air-defense systems over 5G
snippet: Ericsson has demonstrated the use of a tactical 5G network to wirelessly interconnect counter-drone and air-defense systems The post Ericsson demos counter-drone and air-defense systems over 5G appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Press Release

Ericsson has demonstrated the use of a tactical 5G network to wirelessly interconnect counter-drone and air-defense systems during Atlas 26, the Spanish Armed Forces’ main joint military exercise, focused on responding to unmanned aerial threats, and held from 19 to 23 October at the Médano del Loro training area in Huelva. For the first time the Spanish Armed Forces have connected counter-drone (C-UAS) relying solely on a tactical 5G network, replacing fixed cabling with a highly mobile, rapidly deployable link.

Atlas 26 evaluates the joint response to massive air threats, with a focus on drone, anti-aircraft and missile technologies. Effective coordination depends on sharing data between sensors, radars, command posts and effector systems quickly and reliably. Until now, that interconnection relied on physical cabling, which constrains how quickly forces can reposition and scale on the ground.

The demonstration used Ericsson Ultra Compact Core, a compact, mobile, defense-grade and rapidly deployable 5G Core. The deployment featured a pre-integrated solution comprising Ericsson 5G Core software, the Ericsson Container-as-a-Service platform and the necessary hardware infrastructure and was operated by the 5G Spanish Cyber Defense Centre of the Joint Cyberspace Command (Mando Conjunto del Ciberespacio).  Ericsson equipment installed operated in bands reserved exclusively for military use.

The demonstration established a tactical 5G network providing:

Dedicated connectivity isolated from commercial traffic using military-exclusive spectrum.

Reduced exposure to electromagnetic interference and congestion.

Low-latency data exchange between connected systems, supporting the coordination of distributed counter-drone and air-defense capabilities.

Juan Olivera, country manager of Ericsson Spain, says: “This exercise has shown how commercial 5G innovation, hardened for defense, can give armed forces a decisive operational edge. A sovereign, deployable 5G network puts resilient, high-capacity connectivity exactly where it is needed, with no dependence on fixed infrastructure. By linking sensors to effectors in real time, we help defense forces coordinate their systems more effectively and operate with greater flexibility on the ground.”

Tactical 5G provides armed forces with a mobile connectivity layer that can be rapidly deployed and adapted to changing operational conditions. By reducing reliance on fixed cabling and connecting distributed sensors, command-and-control systems and effectors, the Atlas 26 demonstration highlights how tactical 5G can give armed forces greater flexibility to deploy, reposition and connect their systems in the field, providing a practical foundation for its wider adoption across Spain’s and Europe’s future operations.
